# Exceptions

Exceptions are thrown to signal undesired situations. These are a means of
communicating that something didn’t go as expected. For example, if we try to
withdraw more money than we have in our account, the banking application may
throw an exception to indicate that. These exceptions can be logged for further
analysis. Unfortunately, exceptions can be swallowed which means these are not
logged nor propagated up the call stack, as shown in this example. JFR can help
us track all exceptions thrown by an application irrespective of whether these
are logged, propagated up the stack or swallowed.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [`jq`](https://jqlang.org/)

- [`codex`](https://developers.openai.com/codex/)

- [JDK Mission Control (JMC)](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

## JDK Mission Control (JMC)

1. Download the latest version of JMC from
   [here](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

2. Specify the version of Java

   When having multiple versions of Java installed, you may need to specify
   which one to be used by JMC. This can be done through the `jmc.ini` file,
   found under the `Eclipse` directory of where JMC is installed.

   Add the `-vm` option followed by the path to the `bin` directory, as shown
   next.

   ```
   ...
   -vm
   /Users/aattard/.sdkman/candidates/java/current/bin
   ...
   ```

   Please note that this file will contain other information, which is excluded
   for brevity.

## Build the application

The following examples require the application to be built.

```shell
./mvnw clean package
```

(*Optional*) Verify that the JAR file was created.

```shell
tree --sort=name './target/libs'
```

There should be one JAR file.

```
./target/libs
└── exceptions-1.0.0.jar

1 directory, 1 file
```

Some of the following commands dump JFR files into a `jfr` directory. Make sure
that the `jfr` directory exists.

```shell
rm -rf './jfr'
mkdir -p './jfr'
```

## Create custom configuration

This example will analyse exceptions. The exception data is not collected by
either the *default* nor the *profile* configurations. This provides insight on
the number of exceptions thrown and from where. Create a new configuration that
captures the exceptions’ events.

1. Create the custom configuration.

   ```shell
   jfr configure \
     jdk.JavaExceptionThrow#enabled=true \
     --output './jfr/custom.jfc'
   ```

   Alternatively, use the interactive option, as shown below, and follow the
   provided instructions.

   ```shell
   jfr configure --interactive --output './jfr/custom.jfc'
   ```

   When asked about errors, select option `3`, to collect all exceptions, and
   accept the default for the rest.

   ```
   ...
   Exceptions: Errors Only (default)
   1. Off
   2. Errors Only
   3. All Exceptions, including Errors
   3
   Using: All Exceptions, including Errors
   ...
   ```

2. (*Optional*) A `.jfc` file will be created. This file can be saved anywhere
   on the filesystem as long as it is accessible. For this example, the `.jfc`
   is saved under the `jfr` directory.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The custom configuration.

   ```
   ./jfr
   └── custom.jfc

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

   The `.jfr` file is an XML file and can be viewed and edited manually.

## Analyse the exceptions thrown by the application

1. Run the application and start flight recorder with the custom configuration
   (`./jfr/custom.jfc`).

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='Exceptions',filename='./jfr/demo.jfr',settings='./jfr/custom.jfc' \
     -jar './target/libs/exceptions-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

   The application will terminate automatically after 40 seconds.

   (*Optional*) Verify that the JFR file was created.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recording.

   ```
   ./jfr
   ├── custom.jfc
   └── demo.jfr

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. Open the recording file (`./jfr/demo.jfr`), in JDK Mission Control.

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo.jfr"
   ```

   The dashboard immediately indicates that our application is throwing a lot of
   exceptions.

   ![Thrown Exceptions](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Thrown%20Exceptions.png)

   Click on the *Exceptions*.

   Here we can see all the exceptions thrown and from where these were thrown.

   ![Exceptions](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Exceptions.png)

3. Analyse the recording file (`./jfr/demo.jfr`) with a custom program.

   A Java program can open a JFR recording file, analyse each event, and
   identify which exceptions are created (though not necessarily thrown). The
   example below reads the recording file, filters for `jdk.JavaExceptionThrow`
   events, maps each exception and its message, and counts how frequently each
   method appears during sampling.

   ```java
   #!/usr/bin/env -S java --source 25

   import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedClass;
   import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent;
   import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile;

   import java.io.IOException;
   import java.io.UncheckedIOException;
   import java.nio.file.Path;
   import java.util.HashMap;
   import java.util.Map;

   public static void main(final String[] args) {
       if (args.length != 1) {
           System.out.println("Usage: ./PrintExceptions <RECORDING-FILE>");
           System.exit(1);
       }

       final Path path = Path.of(args[0]);
       final Map<ExceptionCreated, Long> results = compute(path);

       results.entrySet().stream()
               .sorted(Map.Entry.<ExceptionCreated, Long>comparingByValue().reversed())
               .limit(20)
               .forEach(entry ->
                       System.out.printf("%5d %-60s %s%n", entry.getValue(),
                       truncate(entry.getKey().type(), 60),
                       entry.getKey().message()));
   }

   private static Map<ExceptionCreated, Long> compute(final Path path) {
       final Map<ExceptionCreated, Long> results = new HashMap<>();

       try (RecordingFile recordingFile = new RecordingFile(path)) {
           while (recordingFile.hasMoreEvents()) {
               final RecordedEvent event = recordingFile.readEvent();

               /* The jdk.ExceptionThrown event in JFR captures the stack trace from the point where the exception
                   object is instantiated, not where it is actually thrown (i.e., the throw statement). */
               if ("jdk.JavaExceptionThrow".equals(event.getEventType().getName())) {
                   final String exceptionType = event.<RecordedClass>getValue("thrownClass").getName();
                   final String message = event.getValue("message");

                   final ExceptionCreated exceptionCreated = new ExceptionCreated(exceptionType, message);
                   results.merge(exceptionCreated, 1L, Long::sum);
               }
           }

           return results;
       } catch (final IOException e) {
           throw new UncheckedIOException("Failed to read recording file " + path, e);
       }
   }

   private record ExceptionCreated(String type, String message) {}

   public static String truncate(final String original, final int maxLength) {
       if (maxLength <= original.length()) {
           return "..." + original.substring(original.length() - maxLength + 3);
       }

       return original;
   }
   ```

   Analyse the recording file.

   ```shell
   ./src/main/java/PrintExceptions './jfr/demo.jfr'
   ```

   The program will print the exceptions that were created.

   ```
    2866 demo.WithdrawMoneyException                                  Not enough money in account
   ```

4. Analyse the exception evidence with AI.

   JFR shows exceptions even when the application catches and swallows them. In
   a real application, the recording tells us which exceptions were created and
   which stack frames were involved, but it does not explain the application’s
   intent. Give Codex the extracted JFR evidence and read-only access to the
   source tree so the agent can follow stack frames into the code and check
   whether exceptions are logged, propagated, handled, or swallowed.

   ```shell
   # Run Codex from an isolated directory that contains the extracted JFR evidence.
   rm -rf 'target/jfr-ai'
   mkdir -p 'target/jfr-ai'

   # Extract the exception events and aggregate repeated failures before sending them to Codex.
   jfr print --json \
     --events 'jdk.JavaExceptionThrow' \
     './jfr/demo.jfr' |
     jq 'def frames: [
           .values.stackTrace.frames[]? | {
             class: .method.type.name,
             method: .method.name,
             line: .lineNumber,
             frameType: .type
           }
         ];
         {
           exceptions: (
             [.recording.events[] | {
               thrownClass: .values.thrownClass.name,
               message: .values.message,
               thread: .values.eventThread.javaName,
               topFrames: (frames[:8])
             }]
             | group_by({thrownClass, message})
             | map({
                 thrownClass: .[0].thrownClass,
                 message: .[0].message,
                 count: length,
                 sampleThread: .[0].thread,
                 sampleFrames: .[0].topFrames
               })
             | sort_by(.count)
             | reverse
           )
         }' > 'target/jfr-ai/exceptions.json'

   codex exec \
     --ephemeral \
     --cd "${PWD}/target/jfr-ai" \
     --add-dir "${PWD}/src/main/java" \
     --sandbox read-only \
     --model gpt-6.1-terra \
     --config 'model_reasoning_effort="medium"' \
     --skip-git-repo-check \
     --output-last-message 'target/jfr-ai/exception-ai-analysis.md' \
     - <<'EOF' > 'target/jfr-ai/exception-ai-run.log' 2>&1
   You are analysing Java Flight Recorder exception events for a workshop.

   Use @exceptions.json as the source of truth for what happened at runtime.
   Use the added source directory to inspect application code referenced by the
   exception stack frames.

   Do not invent events. Do not assume an exception is logged, propagated,
   handled, or swallowed unless the source code supports that conclusion.
   Do not use Markdown links or absolute file paths. When citing source evidence,
   use paths relative to src/main/java, such as demo/FaultyWorker.java:12.

   Identify:
   1. which exception types dominate the recording
   2. which application methods are most closely associated with them
   3. whether the source logs, propagates, handles, or swallows those exceptions
   4. why the exception pattern may be a performance or observability problem
   5. concrete code areas a developer should inspect next

   Return a concise finding list with evidence fields.
   EOF

   cat 'target/jfr-ai/exception-ai-analysis.md'
   ```

   Codex correlates the JFR exception evidence with the source code.

   ```markdown
   1. **One exception type dominates the supplied recording data.**
      - **Runtime evidence:** exceptions.json contains 2,866 events for `demo.WithdrawMoneyException`, accounting for 100% of the listed exceptions. Message: “Not enough money in account”; sample thread: `pool-1-thread-1`.
      - **Limit:** The file provides an aggregate count and sample frames, not a complete stack for every event.

   2. **`FaultyWorker.transferMoney()` is the directly associated application method.**
      - **Runtime evidence:** The sample stack includes `FaultyWorker.transferMoney():28` and `WithdrawMoneyException.<init>():11`.
      - **Source evidence:** demo/FaultyWorker.java:28 constructs and throws the exception when `hasEnoughMoney()` returns false. demo/WithdrawMoneyException.java:11 calls `super(message)`.
      - **Inspect next:** demo/FaultyWorker.java:34—the balance check uses a random boolean, making failure a routine possibility rather than checking an actual account.

   3. **The source propagates the exception to `run()`, which silently swallows it.**
      - **Source evidence:** demo/FaultyWorker.java:12 calls `transferMoney()`; demo/FaultyWorker.java:13 catches `RuntimeException`, with an empty catch body at line 14. There is no logging, recovery action, or rethrow in this path.
      - **Observability concern:** Failures leave no application-level diagnostic here, and the broad catch can also hide other runtime exceptions.
      - **Inspect next:** demo/FaultyWorker.java:13—narrow the catch and explicitly record or handle failed transfers.

   4. **Repeated exception construction may create avoidable performance overhead.**
      - **Runtime evidence:** 2,866 recorded exceptions; the sample includes `Throwable` construction.
      - **Source evidence:** demo/FaultyWorker.java:10 repeats indefinitely, throwing a new exception on failed checks and sleeping only 1 ms between attempts at line 18.
      - **Concern:** Repeated allocation and stack-trace capture may consume CPU and increase garbage collection pressure. These exception data alone do not quantify that cost or establish a bottleneck.
      - **Inspect next:** demo/FaultyWorker.java:26—consider an explicit result for expected insufficient funds; inspect loop pacing at lines 10–18 and correlate with allocation, CPU, and GC events.
   ```
